option.1: Praise from the model, plus invented features and a score out of ten
option.2: Who the person is, where they are, what they want, and what they see
option.3: A one-to-ten rating that replaces questions about the intended problem
option.4: Extra modules the model lists so you can skip naming a real moment
answerExplanation: A test scenario is a short story of a real moment, not a generic user. Praise, scores, and extra-module lists are not scenarios.

contentBody: **How should you brief a chat tool before it role-plays a user?**
option.1: Paste the page text only; do not paste hopes or the idea card
option.2: Paste the idea card first so the model already “gets” the problem
option.3: Ask why the product is great, then treat the praise as proof
option.4: Put every user type in one prompt so the voices blend into a committee
answerExplanation: Simulated feedback should react to what is on the screen. Leaking the idea card, asking for praise, or mixing voices is not a test.

contentBody: **Why simulate one user voice per prompt instead of mixing several?**
option.1: One prompt takes longer, so the model will invent a finished market survey
option.2: Many voices in one reply are treated as proof that real people already agree
option.3: Mixing voices is required so the model can give a score out of ten
option.4: Separate prompts keep reactions distinct; mixing them blends the voices
answerExplanation: One prompt per person keeps the replies from sounding like a committee. Mixing voices, inventing a survey, or forcing a score is not the method.

contentBody: **What should a strong question about the prototype actually test?**
option.1: Whether the logo, colours, and dark mode feel premium enough
option.2: Which extra product lines and funding stories the model can invent
option.3: Whether this version attacks the intended problem, not taste or extras
option.4: Whether a one-to-ten rating can replace yes, maybe, or no plus a reason
answerExplanation: Strong questions check understanding, desire, confusion, and whether the claimed job would actually get easier. Taste, modules, and invented scores do not test that job.

contentBody: **Which statement about simulated user feedback is correct?**
option.1: Detailed chatbot replies equal watching people in the real situation
option.2: It is a rehearsal filter, not proof that real people will use the offer
option.3: If the model writes a long review, you can skip any later real-user test
option.4: A simulated “no” is harder to hear than a real person saying no to a friend
answerExplanation: Simulated replies help you catch fuzzy headlines and weak next steps. They miss real thumbs, trust, and social cost, so detail is not evidence.
